summary.text: Seismic tomography is a way of making pictures of what lies beneath Earth's surface using seismic waves.
The material seismic waves pass through changes them, so comparing recordings made at different places lets scientists build a model of the structure below.
The result is almost always a map of wave speed, whose features can be read as differences in structure, temperature or composition.

facts.label: Modern method arrived
facts.value: The 1970s, as global seismic networks expanded

facts.label: Name borrowed from
facts.value: Medical X-ray tomography, first applied to seismology in 1984

facts.label: Range of scales
facts.value: From the whole Earth down to the top few meters

items.prompt: Imagine Earth's interior were made of exactly the same material everywhere. How would seismic waves travel through it?

options.label: Curving down toward the core
Zigzagging between hidden layers
In straight lines
Bending back up to the surface

items.explain: Waves bend, reflect and refract only because structure, chemistry and temperature vary inside Earth; with uniform material they would go straight.

items.prompt: A worldwide standardized network of seismographs, later a gift to tomography, was first set up mainly because of what?

options.label: Searching for oil and gas
Underground nuclear tests
Warning cities of earthquakes
Forecasting tsunamis at sea

items.explain: Networks like the World-Wide Standardized Seismograph Network were driven at first by underground nuclear tests, then proved valuable for geoscience.

items.prompt: A hospital CT scanner and seismic tomography both turn receiver data into a 3D image by computer. What does the CT scanner have that earthquake seismologists lack?

options.label: A computer that processes the data
A three-dimensional picture at the end
Receivers that record what passes through
Straight rays from a known source

items.explain: CT uses straight X-rays from a known source, while seismologists must handle curved, reflected paths and uncertain earthquake locations.

items.prompt: A team chooses very long-wavelength waves so they can study the deep mantle. What do they give up?

options.label: The waves will never reach that depth
Small features will not show up clearly
The image will show only temperature
Earthquakes will no longer be usable

items.explain: Longer wavelengths go deeper, but waves cannot sense features much smaller than their wavelength, so resolution drops.

items.prompt: A team refines its picture step by step, starting from an initial Earth model that is badly unrealistic. What is the danger?

options.label: The final image may also be unrealistic
The computer will refuse to run at all
The data will be fit perfectly regardless
The seismometers will record the waves wrongly

items.explain: Methods that improve an initial model step by step can produce unrealistic results if that starting model is unreasonable.

items.prompt: Two careful teams invert the same seismic data and end up with somewhat different underground models. How can both be reasonable?

options.label: One of the teams must have miscounted
Seismometers record differently each day
More than one model can match the data
Seismic waves travel at random speeds

items.explain: Tomographic inversions are non-unique: different models can give a similarly good fit between predictions and observations.
